10.07.2015 in W.P.No.21216/2014 and connected writ petitions whereby writ petitions are allowed,
striking down the Karnataka Private Aided Educational Institutions Employees (Regulation of Pay,
Pension and Other Benefits) Act, 2014 (for short, 'Act No. 7 of 2014'), holding that the Act No.7 of
2014 is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India and encroaches upon the jurisdictional
powers of the Courts, with a further direction to the State to continue to pay salary or pension as the

in W.P.No.105439/2014 and W.P.No.108382-417/2014, whereby the learned Single Judge allowed
the writ petitions, quashed the impugned Act No.4 of 2015 i.e., the Karnataka Education
Amendment Act, 2014 (for short, 'Act No. 4 of 2015'), amendment to Section 87 of Karnataka
Education Act, 1983 (for short, 'Act, 1983') with a further direction to the State to consider the cases
of the petitioners to grant additional increment for passing Kannada Language Examination, in

to Act No.7 of 2014, whereunder, Section 3 would state that, notwithstanding anything contained in

55. Lastly, learned Additional Advocate Generals appearing on behalf of the State contended that the
State would be put to great financial difficulties if the impugned Acts are struck down and any

on the financial capabilities of the State. When the teachers and other employees of private
educational institutions discharge the same duties and responsibilities as that of similarly situated

would be entitled to the same benefit which are extended to the teachers of Government educational
institutions. On the ground of financial constraints or difficulty, persons discharging identical and
similar duties cannot be treated unequally. Article 14 of the Constitution of India endeavors that the
State shall not deny any person equality before law or equal protection of laws. A legislation which
treats similarly situated persons unequally is liable to be struck down as violative of Article 14 of the

Anwar Ali Sarkar, (1952) 1 SCC 1 : AIR 1952 SC 75] The difference is capable of being

the qualifications required and the duties and responsibilities of both employees of aided
institutions and Government servants are the same. Thus, the impugned Acts fail the first test i.e.,
existence of an intelligible C/W 101 OTHERS differentia which distinguishes persons grouped
together from others left out of the group.

58. The aforesaid decision lays down that mere financial constraints or burden on the State
exchequer cannot be a reason to deny a benefit to a similarly situated employee. A perusal of the
Statement of Objects and Reasons appended to Act No. 7 of 2014 and Act No. 5 of 2015 would
indicate that the predominant object behind the enactment of the impugned Acts was to avoid the
substantial financial liability that would arise upon implementation of the orders/judgments
rendered by this Court. However, once it has been held that the employees of private aided
educational institutions are similarly situated to government employees, possessing the same
qualifications and discharging identical duties, mere financial difficulties cannot amount to a
constitutionally permissible basis for denying them parity in service benefits. Consequently, even
assuming that the impugned enactments disclose an intelligible differentia, the object sought to be

with the objects sought to be achieved by the law and hence, are liable to be struck down on this
ground as well.

apart grant-in-aid. Both the above Sections read harmoniously require the State to maintain the

the bounden responsibility of the State to provide similar benefit in all respects that are available to
State Government teachers to that of teachers of private educational institutions, that too, when the
private educational institutions are discharging the duties and responsibilities of State in the matter
of imparting education.

61. It is also necessary to clarify the extent of the relief that would flow from the present judgment.
The issue involved in the present batch of matters is confined to whether the service rendered by
employees during the non-grant period is liable to be reckoned for the purpose of fixation of pay and
other consequential service benefits. Neither the provisions C/W 101 OTHERS governing
grant-in-aid nor the statutory framework casts any liability upon the State to pay salary for the
period prior to admission of the post to grant-in-aid. As produced supra, Annexure-I of Rules, 1999
would make it abundantly clear that the management shall be liable for payment of salary and other
benefits till the date such posts are admitted into grant- in-aid. The liability to pay salary during the
non-grant period continues to rest upon the management of the concerned institution.
Consequently, the service rendered during the said period shall be taken into account only for the
purpose of notional fixation of pay as on the date of admission of the post to grant-in-aid and for
extending consequential benefits such as pension and other service benefits. The employees shall
not be entitled to claim arrears of salary or any other monetary benefits from the State for the period
preceding the admission of the post to grant-in-aid.
